draft.title: How archaeologists study the past
card: Excavate
to dig a site carefully, layer by layer, and record where each find lies.
Artefacts
objects made or used by people, such as tools, pottery and jewellery. Studying them shows how people lived.
Carbon dating
a method of finding the age of once-living material, such as bone, wood or charcoal, by measuring the carbon left in it.
Conserve
to protect sites and objects from damage and decay, so the evidence is kept for people in the future.
draft.remember: Archaeologists dig, study and date finds, and conserve them so the evidence lasts.

a.q: Why do archaeologists record exactly where each find lies as they dig?
opts: Its position helps show how it was used and its age
It makes the dig finish faster
It means the find cannot be damaged
It lets them skip the dating of the find
a.why: Excavating layer by layer and recording each position helps show how a find relates to the others around it. Recording does not protect a find from damage, and it does not replace dating.
a.clue: Think about what the position can tell you.

b.q: Archaeologists find a charcoal fireplace and a stone axe at a campsite. They want to know how old the camp is. Which step helps most?
opts: Carbon dating the charcoal
Carbon dating the stone axe
Conserving the campsite
Taking the axe to a museum
b.why: Charcoal was once living wood, so carbon dating can measure its age. Stone was never alive, so it cannot be carbon dated, and conserving or moving finds does not give an age.
b.clue: Carbon dating needs material that was once alive.

a.best: Its position helps show how it was used and its age

problems.detail: The card says archaeologists record where each find lies, but never says why. The idea that position shows a find's use and age (layers, context) is not taught, so the question needs more than the card gives.
The right option is clearly the longest and the only one with precise detail. The other three are short and obviously silly, so a student could pick it without knowing the idea.

Why (a) explains that position shows how a find relates to the finds around it. It does not support the option's claim about use and age, so the explanation and the intended answer do not quite match.

proposal.title: How archaeologists study the past
card: Excavate
to dig a site carefully, layer by layer, and record which layer each find lies in. Layers build up over time, so deeper layers are usually older than the ones above them.
Artefacts
objects made or used by people, such as tools, pottery and jewellery. Studying them shows how people lived.
Carbon dating
a method of finding the age of once-living material, such as bone, wood or charcoal, by measuring the carbon left in it.
Conserve
to protect sites and objects from damage and decay, so the evidence is kept for people in the future.
proposal.remember: Archaeologists dig, study and date finds, and conserve them so the evidence lasts.

a.q: At a dig, an archaeologist finds a coin in a deep layer and a clay pot in a layer above it. What does this suggest?
opts: The coin is likely older than the pot
The pot is likely older than the coin
The coin and pot are likely the same age
The pot was likely made by the coin's owner
a.why: Layers build up over time, so deeper layers are usually older. The coin lies below the pot, so it is likely older. Saying the pot is older gets the rule the wrong way round.
a.clue: Which layer was laid down first?

b.q: Archaeologists find a charcoal fireplace and a stone axe at a campsite. They want to know how old the camp is. Which step helps most?
opts: Carbon dating the charcoal
Carbon dating the stone axe
Conserving the campsite
Taking the axe to a museum
b.why: Charcoal was once living wood, so carbon dating can measure its age. Stone was never alive, so it cannot be carbon dated, and conserving or moving finds does not give an age.
b.clue: Carbon dating needs material that was once alive.

wants.why: Seeing the layers stacked helps students understand why deeper finds are usually older.
